title: The permissive decree, though not effective, is efficacious; God wills that evil come about
source_text: XXVII. Attamen decretum illud quo malum, qua tale, Deus permittere statuit, licet non effectivum, efficax tamen esse volunt: unde est quod omnia quae fiunt, tam bona quam mala, tribuunt decreto Dei, ut graeca voce vocant, energetico, quod postea subdividunt in effectivum & efficax. Nam juxta ipsos, non minus necesse est ut posito Dei decreto permissivo, malum Deo permittente fiat; quam posito Dei decreto effectivo, necesse est ut fiat bonum Deo probante & efficiente. Adeoque pertendunt vere dici posse & debere non solum quod Deus malum permittere velit, sed etiam quod velit malum fieri ipso permittente: Quia, scilicet, divina voluntas non tantum fertur in mali permissionem, sed etiam in eventum ipsius actionis malae.
pass_a_gloss: XXVII. Yet they will that decree by which God determined to permit evil, as such, though not effective, to be nevertheless efficacious: whence it is that all things which are done, both good and evil, they attribute to the decree of God, as they call it by a Greek word, energetic, which they afterwards subdivide into effective and efficacious. For according to them, it is no less necessary that, God's permissive decree being posited, evil be done by God permitting; than, God's effective decree being posited, it is necessary that good be done by God approving and effecting. And so they insist that it can and ought truly to be said not only that God wills to permit evil, but also that he wills evil to be done, he himself permitting: Because, namely, the divine will is borne not only to the permission of evil, but also to the event of the evil action itself.
pass_b_english: Yet they hold that the decree by which God resolved to permit evil as such, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious. That is why they ascribe everything that is done, good and evil alike, to God's decree which they call, with a Greek word, 'energetic', and which they then subdivide into effective and efficacious.

On their view, once God's permissive decree is in place, it is no less necessary that evil be done with God permitting it than, once his effective decree is in place, that good be done with God approving and bringing it about.

So they insist that it can and should truly be said not only that God wills to permit evil, but also that he wills evil to be done by his permission. The reason is that the divine will is directed not only to permitting evil but also to the actual outcome of the evil action.
